You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC demo discipline

## Workflow
1. Parse each region, background, object colors, divider orientation, and dimensions from the current instance. Treat task IDs and remembered task-specific rules as hypotheses only; recurring tasks may vary in geometry and palette.
2. Compare every demo input-output pair cell-by-cell. Identify equality/inequality mappings, output palette, row/column orientation, and unchanged cases. Explain all observations with one consistent rule before submitting.
3. Choose demos by information value. If candidate rules remain ambiguous and a wrong submission costs more than a demo, request a demo that distinguishes them. Do not spend attempts on speculative palette or orientation variants.
4. After an incorrect submission, explicitly discard the hypothesis it tested. Reassess all of the test and demos; do not repeat uniform grids, near-identical masks, or cosmetic color changes. Before a later submission, verify each output coordinate, dimensions, and palette against the rule and examples.
5. Maintain the interface contract on every turn: output exactly one valid JSON action object on the final line, with no explanation or extra text. Valid actions are `submit`, `request_demos`, or `finish` only when the instance is over. Do not use `finish` prematurely.

Test consists of multiple isolated outlined rectangles with blank interiors and a few singleton-marker interiors. Four demos in this exact instance established a strong local transformation: preserve frame borders/exterior; recolor blank strict interiors to 2, while a single-cell marked interior becomes 7. Demo 1: bg8, 4-frame interior 2x2 ->2; 0-frame 4x4->2; 0-frame 6x6->2; 9-frame singleton marker ->7. Demo 2: 9-frame 2x2->2, 8-frame 4x5->7, 1-frame 3x3->7. Demo 3: 9-frame 2x2->2 and 8-frame 2x2->2. Demo 4: 3-frame 4x4->2; 6-frame 2x2->2; 8-frame singleton->7. Thus both interior contents and/or outer dimensions/context may matter; blank interiors commonly map 2, singleton maps 7, but demo 2's large blank 4x5 interior mapped 7 and blocks a simple blank->2 rule.

Test features (0-indexed): frame color1 rows0-2 cols19-21, singleton center (1,20); frame color1 rows4-11 cols10-17 with strict interior rows5-10 cols11-16 (6x6 blank); frame color4 rows4-8 cols22-26, interior rows5-7 cols23-25 (3x3 blank); frame color6 rows10-12 cols0-2, singleton center (11,1); frame color9 rows11-13 cols5-7, singleton center (12,6); frame color3 rows10-13 cols22-25, interior rows11-12 cols23-24 (2x2 blank). Eight rejected outputs all preserved shapes and variously filled subsets with 2 and/or 7; no rule obtained. ### Solved 11x18 instance: recolor all closed frame interiors by area parity
Preserve frame borders and exterior/background. Fill every strict rectangular interior: odd number of interior cells -> color 7; even number -> color 2. Demos confirmed 1x1, 3x3, 5x5 interiors -> 7; 2x2, 4x4, 6x6 -> 2. The proven invariant is interior-cell-count parity; observed interiors happened to be squares.

Solved test had THREE frames, including an easy-to-miss large color-3 frame: color-5 frame rows1-3, cols0-2 had 1x1 interior at (2,1) ->7; color-8 frame rows6-9, cols1-4 had 2x2 interior rows7-8, cols2-3 ->2; color-3 frame rows0-7, cols6-13 had 6x6 interior rows1-6, cols7-12 ->2. All other cells/borders unchanged. Accepted output was submitted in this session.

Failure lesson: the first three rejected submissions omitted the large frame's 6x6 interior (and varied fills on the two small interiors). The successful submission recolored all three. Always scan the entire grid for every enclosed frame, including large ones; do not stop after the obvious small objects. Historical task notes can conflict across recurrences; the above is confirmed for this instance by the demos and accepted answer.
A current 28x23 instance contains outlined rectangles with interiors: color-0 outline at rows 8-11, cols 7-10 (2x2 interior); color-3 outline rows 9-11 cols 17-19 (1x1 interior); color-4 outline rows 14-20 cols 15-21 (5x5 interior); color-5 outlines rows 17-20 cols 0-3 (2x2), rows 16-19 cols 5-8 (2x2), rows 18-20 cols 11-13 (1x1); color-8 outline rows 22-24 cols 12-14 (1x1). Do not repeat a size-only palette rule. Request demos and compare rectangle outline color, interior size, location/context, and neighboring shapes; preserve outlines/background.

## task-38f52b9d recurrence: solid separator lines recolored 2

### Accepted 20x12 test (0 wrong)
Input was an 18x12 grid, palette 8/9, with a complete uniform row pair of 8 at rows 13–14 (0-based) and a full-height vertical separator column 3 of 8. Accepted output changed every cell in those rows and that column to 2, leaving all other cells unchanged. Use the task's separator-line rule supported by demonstrations: recolor full uniform structural rows and identified recurring vertical separator column(s) to 2; preserve all other cells. Do not globally recolor all uniform columns. In this test, detected lines are rows 13,14 and column 3. This accepted recurrence confirms the row+column transformation for palette 8/9.

## task-38f52b9d: separator lines and special column recoloring (demo-confirmed)

### Accepted recurrence: 14x7 sparse separator column
Input was 14x7, mostly rows `[6,6,0,6,6,6,6]`, with fully uniform all-0 rows at indices 10 and 13. Accepted transformation: recolor every cell of the recurring vertical separator column (column 2, zero-based; all its 0s) to 2, and recolor each full-width uniform separator row to 2. Preserve all other cells exactly. This produced rows `[6,6,2,6,6,6,6]` except rows 10 and 13, which became all 2. This confirms the compact separator-line recurrence: identify the structural column/row lines from repeated aligned separators, recolor them to 2; do not recolor other cells.

Rule: Recolor every full uniform row to 2. Full uniform rows include both separator rows (background color) and any uniform rows of the other color; do not recolor uniform columns wholesale. In addition, recolor the distinguished column to 2: demos establish this as the column whose input color matches the separator color / recurring separator-line color, while preserving all its non-uniform line companions (only the cells in that column change). In Demo 2 (12x25), every all-6 row became all 2; columns 0,4,8,14,20 were all 6 in the input and became 2, reflecting the recurring vertical separators (not arbitrary uniform columns—some columns with other values remain untouched). Demo 3 (24x24) confirms full uniform rows all 8 -> 2 and two internal vertical lines c10 and c16 of 8 -> 2, while other 8 markers remain unchanged. Thus detect the grid's structural vertical separator column(s) from repeated aligned full-height / near-full-height columns of the separator color, rather than changing all columns of any uniform color. In the solved test (20x10), rows 3,4,5,8,10 were uniform 6 and became 2; column 4 was the internal separator, all 6 there became 2; every other cell stayed exactly as input. A further accepted recurrence (9x18, palette 3/9) has uniform rows 3 and 5 (0-based), and full-height uniform columns 2 (all 3) and 17 (all 3). The correct transformation recolors those full uniform rows and columns to 2, preserving every other cell. This recurrence confirms full uniform columns can be part of the separator structure; in the test, columns 2 and 17 were both entirely 3. Rejected hypothesis: globally recoloring every uniform column is incorrect in examples with structural separator selection; identify columns supported by current demo patterns. Validate output dimensions and preserve all remaining pixels.

Earlier resolved recurrence memory had an overgeneralized “recolor all uniform rows and columns” claim; treat it as superseded. The demonstrations show aligned separator structure, not a simple uniform-line rule for columns.


## Paired-band comparison pattern
When a solid full-width row or full-height column separates two aligned bands, exclude the divider and compare corresponding cells. A common learned mapping is equality => 3 and inequality => the first band's background; determine that background from the full band rather than assuming its most visually prominent color. Horizontal divider: compare upper/lower bands; vertical divider: compare left/right. Confirm the exact palette and mapping from current demos rather than importing this pattern blindly.
